documents.title: Design and write AI policies
documents.summary: CATLOE guidance that walks instructors through deciding whether AI helps the skills their course targets, writing a policy that explains the reasons, and opening a class conversation. It offers sample policy text and four conversation plans but no university-wide rule.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule on AI use. It says "each instructor will need to do this work for each course they teach" and offers a three-phase framework, so the decision is handed to instructors.

units.why: The guide says "each instructor will need to do this work for each course they teach", so the course rule is set by each instructor, not borrowed or set centrally; addressed to instructors, before the course, hence P04.
units.anchor: each instructor will need to do this work for each course they teach
units.frag_start: While it might be tempting
units.fit_note: Also warns against copying another instructor's policy.

units.why: "Courses, disciplines, and learning goals differ, and these differences have implications for whether, when, or how students should be using AI" ties the AI decision to learning goals, which is P83 (not P04, because the point is the basis of the decision).
units.anchor: these differences have implications for whether, when, or how students should be using AI
units.frag_start: Courses, disciplines, and learning goals

units.why: Policies are reframed as "an opportunity for instructors to consider how they want learning to happen" rather than rules that "reward or punish". No existing type covers a principle about the purpose of a policy, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: a more productive way to think about a course policy
units.frag_start: Traditionally, many instructors have thought
units.frag_end: explore and commit to how they best learn
units.uncovered_note: Course AI policies should be conceived as guides for student learning rather than as rules that reward or punish behavior.

units.why: "we need to start by exploring and articulating for ourselves whether or not artificial intelligence is a meaningful tool for our students" makes the AI decision follow from the skills taught, so P83; addressed to instructors before the course.
units.anchor: whether or not artificial intelligence is a meaningful tool for our students to use
units.frag_start: before we design a policy about AI

units.why: Step 1 tells instructors to "Identify the key skills you want students to learn in your course" as the first step of policy design; it feeds the learning-objectives basis for AI decisions (P83).
units.anchor: Identify the key skills you want students to learn in your course
units.frag_start: Step 1: Identify the key skills
units.fit_note: A procedural step that precedes the AI decision rather than a rule about AI itself.

units.why: "The question is not whether students could use AI to do this work, but instead if using AI will help them develop the skill" sets the test for allowing AI: whether it helps develop a skill, so P83.
units.anchor: if using AI will help them develop the skill
units.frag_start: The question is not whether students could use AI

units.why: Step 3 asks instructors to "articulate for yourself why you think the use of artificial intelligence might help or hinder your students' learning"; it is reasoning behind the AI decision tied to learning, P83.
units.anchor: articulate for yourself
units.frag_start: After you've considered whether using AI
units.fit_note: Asks for the instructor's private articulation of reasons, not the decision itself.

units.why: Example reasoning for a "no": "They won't be able to evaluate the suggestions AI would make unless they have their own strongly developed sense" says learners without skill cannot judge AI output, matching P42.
units.anchor: They won't be able to evaluate the suggestions AI would make
units.frag_start: In cases where you answer no
units.fit_note: Illustrative example of an instructor's rationale for no AI in an editing skill, not a university rule.

units.why: The "yes" example says "it is okay for students to use AI to generate initial ideas for essays/projects", a permission for idea generation, P15.
units.anchor: it is okay for students to use AI to generate initial ideas for essays/projects
units.frag_start: In cases where you answer yes
units.fit_note: Given as a sample rationale an instructor might write.

units.why: The same example adds the condition that students be "aware that this partner is limited, sometimes wrong or biased, and might hallucinate", an instruction to treat AI output critically (P31).
units.anchor: aware that this partner is limited, sometimes wrong or biased, and might hallucinate
units.frag_start: In cases where you answer yes

units.why: "explain to your students when you want them to use AI and when you don't want them to use AI" tells instructors to state their AI expectations to students, which P09 covers; a communication step, so course-start.
units.anchor: when you want them to use AI and when you don't want them
units.frag_start: Using your ideas from Step 1
units.fit_note: Guidance, not a mandate, and does not name the syllabus specifically.

units.why: "explain to your students the reasons that you do or don't want them to use AI" asks instructors to give reasons behind their AI rules, which is P66.
units.anchor: the reasons that you do or don't want them to use AI
units.frag_start: Using your ideas from Step 3
units.frag_end: the learning you want them to do.

units.why: "Communicate this in terms of the assignments in your course (both formative and summative)" says to tie the AI rule to specific assignments, closest to P09 (state expectations in assignment instructions).
units.anchor: Communicate this in terms of the assignments in your course
units.frag_start: Communicate this in terms
units.fit_note: Also suggests framing the rule by the skills the course targets.

units.why: The sample policy states "AI is not a productive technology to use in the research process for our course", discouraging AI for one skill without a formal ban, so P03; it is an example the guide models for instructors.
units.anchor: AI is not a productive technology to use in the research process for our course
units.frag_start: Our course helps you develop
units.fit_note: Sample course policy text embedded in the guidance, not a university rule.

units.why: In the sample policy, "If you lean into AI, you won't develop these skills" gives the reason for limiting AI: it shortcuts the practice that builds skill, P41.
units.anchor: If you lean into AI, you won't develop these skills
units.frag_start: If you lean into AI

units.why: The sample says "I will structure your use of the technology" to give feedback on arguments, i.e. instructor-structured, assignment-specific AI use; an assignment built around AI (P35) rather than a general permission.
units.anchor: I will structure your use of the technology as you do this
units.frag_start: However, we can use AI to provide feedback
units.fit_note: Sample course policy: AI is allowed only as an instructor-structured feedback tool on historical arguments.

units.why: "your policy needs to be framed as an inviting appeal" asks instructors to word the rule with care and in terms of learning, which P66 covers (wording the rules with care).
units.anchor: your policy needs to be framed as an inviting appeal
units.frag_start: This means your policy needs

units.why: "Describe how you will help them regulate their behavior and the temptation to use AI when it is not appropriate" asks instructors to reduce the pressures behind misuse (e.g. "many low-stakes assessments"), which is P99.
units.anchor: help them regulate their behavior and the temptation to use AI
units.frag_start: Describe how you will help them

units.why: The sample statement says "you will get plenty of support during this course, so you don't need to use AI inappropriately", showing how to ease pressure by pointing to course support; P99 rather than P72 because it is about preventing misuse.
units.anchor: you will get plenty of support during this course
units.frag_start: But you don't need to use it anywhere else
units.fit_note: Sample course policy text; also points to peers and instructor as human support.

units.why: "Use your policy to begin this conversation: explore and discuss your policy and/or artificial intelligence in your discipline with students" asks instructors to discuss the rules in class, P66.
units.anchor: explore and discuss your policy and/or artificial intelligence in your discipline with students
units.frag_start: Use your policy to begin this conversation

units.why: Conversation plan 1: "Ask students to read your policy and then write down two things they find helpful and two genuine questions" is a concrete way to discuss the rules, P66.
units.anchor: Ask students to read your policy and then write down two things they find helpful
units.frag_start: Ask students to read your policy

units.why: Conversation plan 2: "it is important that you give them an opportunity to consider how doing work without artificial intelligence will help them learn" asks instructors who ban AI to let students weigh the reasons; P66.
units.anchor: an opportunity to consider how doing work without artificial intelligence will help them learn
units.frag_start: If you don't want students to use AI

units.why: Conversation plan 3: "You may want to explore the uses and limitations of AI with your students" by comparing AI and human arguments; a class discussion of AI (P66), closest type, though it also teaches AI limits.
units.anchor: explore the uses and limitations of AI with your students
units.frag_start: You may want to explore
units.fit_note: Teaching about AI limitations through an in-class analytic activity, not just explaining a rule.

units.why: Plan 4: "students can and should negotiate their use of AI with you (and perhaps with each other)" has instructors set AI use together with students, P67.
units.anchor: students can and should negotiate their use of AI with you

documents.title: Addressing Dishonesty and AI
documents.summary: CATLOE guide giving eight course-design practices to reduce cheating on essays, including with ChatGPT: low-stakes work, clear value of assessments, preparation, feedback, student choice, specific assessments, and critiquing AI text. It has no detection, sanction or AI rule content.
documents.stance_why: The page states no rule on AI use; it gives instructors "eight such practices" to "minimize student cheating", so decisions and actions rest with instructors.

units.why: The page says students "will be tempted to take shortcuts that will rob them of valuable learning opportunities", a rationale that AI shortcuts undermine skill-building: P41.
units.anchor: take shortcuts that will rob them of valuable learning opportunities
units.frag_start: Plagiarism in college essay

units.why: "research-based practices that can be used to minimize student cheating on essays and papers" sets the guide's approach as prevention by course design; P99 fits better than P36 since no sanction is described.
units.anchor: research-based practices that can be used to minimize student cheating on essays and papers
units.frag_start: The good news is that there are multiple
units.fit_note: Covers cheating in general (papers, ChatGPT), not AI only.

units.why: "consider smaller, more frequent essays that carry less weight for students' final average" recommends changing grading weights to reduce the incentive to cheat, P35.
units.anchor: consider smaller, more frequent essays that carry less weight
units.frag_start: you should consider two alternatives
units.fit_note: Also states the pressure rationale: students may cheat when a single assessment decides success (P99).

units.why: "small writing assignments that build toward a larger essay" with revision after feedback is a second redesign of assignments to deter cheating, P35.
units.anchor: small writing assignments that build toward a larger essay
units.frag_start: Second, and perhaps even more effectively

units.why: "It is important to share with students how the assessment will benefit them" asks instructors to explain the reasons for an assessment, which P66 covers.
units.anchor: It is important to share with students how the assessment will benefit them
units.frag_start: When students see assessments
units.fit_note: Concerns assignments in general, not an AI rule specifically.

units.why: "make sure that there are multiple opportunities for students to practice using the skills that assessment requires" aims to reduce anxiety that makes students "more likely to cheat", prevention of misuse pressure: P99.
units.anchor: make sure that there are multiple opportunities for students to practice
units.frag_start: As you design course activities
units.frag_end: value of that practice to them.

units.why: "structure self-regulatory preparatory work right into your class" (planning for papers) is advice to reduce unpreparedness that drives cheating, P99.
units.anchor: structure self-regulatory preparatory work right into your class
units.frag_start: The best way to work against this feeling

units.why: "Help these students by having them analyze their efforts and the feedback you provide" targets the panic after a low grade that leads to cheating, a prevention step, P99.
units.anchor: Help these students by having them analyze their efforts and the feedback you provide
units.frag_start: Help these students by having them

units.why: "Allow students to choose the focus of their writing based on real interests" is an assignment redesign claimed to make cheating less likely, P35.
units.anchor: students can choose a topic of interest to them
units.frag_start: If your course design involves a paper or project
units.frag_end: explore their own thinking more fully.

units.why: "creating assessments that are very specific to your discipline, your course" makes it harder to use others' work "in lieu of their own"; this is assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: creating assessments that are very specific to your discipline, your course
units.frag_start: A key practice that makes it more difficult

units.why: "have them thoughtfully evaluate the writing it generates" recommends students critique ChatGPT output to "strengthen their resolve to resist shortcuts"; an assignment designed around AI, P35.
units.anchor: having them thoughtfully evaluate the writing it generates
units.frag_start: We can, however, strengthen their resolve
units.fit_note: Also builds critical evaluation of AI output (P31).

units.why: "be sure your assignments are still aligned with the learning goals" ties any AI classroom use to learning objectives, P83.
units.anchor: be sure your assignments are still aligned with the learning goals
units.frag_start: As you consider how you can help

units.why: After revealing the AI source, "have students individually write down the specific weaknesses they see in this writing" and the value of doing their own writing is a teaching activity explaining why to do one's own work, closest to P66.
units.anchor: write down the specific weaknesses they see in this writing
units.frag_start: Then have students individually
units.fit_note: An in-class reflection activity about AI weaknesses and the value of doing one's own writing.

notes: Both documents are teaching-center advice, not rules; most units are 'should' guidance to instructors. The dishonesty page is about cheating on essays in general and mentions AI mainly in practice 8. Sample policy text inside the design page was coded as example units.
